title: I'll Be Collateral for Him — Standing Surety, Letting Go, the Seating Order
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. Today I want to start with a question about teams. When something goes wrong and somebody has to carry it, how many different sentences have you heard people say?
"Look, let's do it this way — you go." "That one's his responsibility." "I said right at the start we shouldn't have done it like this."
In Genesis chapter 43 a whole family is stuck fast: if they do not go down to Egypt they will starve to death, and if they do go, they must hand over Benjamin.

In the last chapter Reuben said, "Kill my two sons, if I don't bring him to you" — and what he put up as security was somebody else. In this chapter Judah says, "I'll be collateral for him. From my hand will you require him … then let me bear the blame forever" — and what he puts up is himself.
So the question this lesson puts to you is this: when it comes round to you, do you say, "Put it on my account", or do you say, "Then you go"?
"The famine was severe in the land. When they had eaten up the grain which they had brought out of Egypt, their father said to them, 'Go again, buy us a little more food.'" (Genesis 43:1–2)
The word behind "severe" is כָּבֵד (*kaved*), and its root sense is "heavy" — the very same root as the word for "glory", כָּבוֹד (*kavod*). The famine is lying on this household like a stone.
And notice the way Jacob says it: "Go again, buy us a little more food." As though nothing whatever had happened on the last trip.
Some older members of a family are exactly like this. The hard thing is sitting right there in the room; he will not discuss it; he only says, "You lot work something out."
Judah spells it out: "The man solemnly warned us, saying, 'You shall not see my face, unless your brother is with you.'"
"Solemnly warned" is הָעֵד הֵעִד (*ha'ed he'id*), the infinitive absolute doubled up, and the force of it is enormous — he warned us, and warned us again, in the gravest terms he had.
"You shall not see my face" is court language, the language of a royal audience. To see the king's face is to be received in favour; not to see it is to be turned away.
Then Jacob says, "Why did you treat me so badly, telling the man that you had another brother?" (Genesis 43:6)
"Treat me so badly" — הֲרֵעֹתֶם (*hare'otem*). Once again the word is me. This father's first reaction is still what all of this has cost him.
And then comes the turning point of the whole chapter. In verse 8, Judah steps forward:

"Send the boy with me, and we'll get up and go, so that we may live, and not die, both we, and you, and also our little ones. I'll be collateral for him. From my hand will you require him. If I don't bring him to you, and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever." (Genesis 43:8–9)

Look at the order in which he says it. The first thing out of his mouth is not himself — it is "both we, and you, and also our little ones." He makes his father see that this is not merely a question about Benjamin; it is the lives of every grandchild in the house.

Then he says it: I myself will be collateral for him. In Hebrew the pronoun "I", אָנֹכִי (*anochi*), could perfectly well have been left out — the verb already carries it. Putting it in makes the sentence say, "I — I will do it."
"I'll be collateral for him" is אֶעֶרְבֶנּוּ (*e'ervenu*), a commercial term: to put yourself up as the pledge, the security, the thing the creditor may seize.
"Then let me bear the blame forever" is וְחָטָאתִי לְךָ כָּל־הַיָּמִים (*vechatati lecha kol-hayamim*), literally "then I shall have sinned against you all my days."

Brothers and sisters, that is not paying compensation. That is paying with yourself. Standing surety, by definition, is not guaranteeing somebody else's sentence with a word of your own; it is staking your whole life on that one sentence.
And who is it saying this? It is the very man who, twenty-two years earlier, proposed, "Come, and let's sell him to the Ishmaelites."
From selling a brother for twenty pieces of silver to trading himself for a brother — what lies in between is chapter 38, the chapter in which he learned to say, "I was the one in the wrong."
Real change begins with one honest admission that you were wrong. Owning it is not the finishing line. It is the starting line.
Reuben made an offer too. Why is Judah's different this time?

In the last chapter Reuben said, "Kill my two sons, if I don't bring him to you" — what he put up as security was somebody else. In this chapter Judah says, "I'll be collateral for him. From my hand will you require him … then let me bear the blame forever" — what he puts up is himself. "I'll be collateral" is a commercial term in Hebrew; it means handing yourself over as the pledge. And "let me bear the blame forever" is literally "then I shall have sinned against you all my days." So standing surety, by definition, is not guaranteeing somebody else's sentence with a word of your own; it is staking your whole life on that sentence. The person in a team who can genuinely carry things is never the one who talks the biggest. It is the one who is willing to have the cost written down under his own name.
How did Judah ever become this kind of man?

The man saying these words is the very one who, twenty-two years earlier, proposed, "Come, and let's sell him to the Ishmaelites." From selling a brother for twenty pieces of silver to trading himself for a brother — what lies in between is chapter 38, the chapter in which he said out loud and in front of everybody, "She is more righteous than I", and so learned to say, "I was the one in the wrong." That line gives us an enormously important hope: real change begins with one honest admission of being wrong. Owning it is not the finishing line; it is the starting line. So if there is something in you today that you cannot bring yourself to say out loud, you do not have to wait until you have improved before you admit it. Admit it first — that is where change is given somewhere to happen.
Is there anything to learn from the way he persuades his father?

Look at the order in which he says it. The first thing out of his mouth is not himself, and it is not Benjamin either — it is "both we, and you, and also our little ones", so that they may live and not die. He makes his father see that this is not a question about one child; it is the lives of every grandchild in the house. Only then does he say, I myself will be collateral for him — and in Hebrew that "I" could have been left out altogether; putting it in makes the sentence say, "I — I will do it." This is an excellent model of how to speak: put the whole picture on the table first, then state your own responsibility plainly, without accusing anyone and without dragging up old accounts. Set that beside the father, whose first words were, "Why did you treat me so badly?" The difference between the two ways of speaking can be heard the moment they are said.
2. A Light from the Original: If I Am Bereaved of My Children, I Am Bereaved
And then there is Jacob. This father, who has spent a whole lifetime grasping, finally opens his hand.

He begins with a set of thoroughly practical measures. He tells them to take the choice fruits of the land — "a little balm, a little honey, spices and myrrh, nuts, and almonds"; to take double money in their hand; to carry back the money that had been returned in the mouth of their sacks; and he even gives the other side a way out of the awkwardness: "Perhaps it was an oversight."
"The choice fruits of the land" is מִזִּמְרַת הָאָרֶץ (*mizimrat ha'aretz*), and that word shares a root with the verb for singing — the praise of that land, the very best it has to show for itself.
And then he says two sentences:
"May God Almighty give you mercy before the man, that he may release to you your other brother and Benjamin. If I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved." (Genesis 43:14)

"God Almighty" is אֵל שַׁדַּי (*El Shaddai*). Every time that name surfaces in Genesis the moment is a decisive one: in chapter 17 God cuts his covenant with Abraham — "I am God Almighty. Walk before me and be blameless" — and in chapter 35, at Bethel, God says to Jacob himself, "I am God Almighty."
He reaches for the covenant name. What he is saying is: this is beyond my managing now; I am handing it over to the God who once spoke to me.
"Mercy" is רַחֲמִים (*rachamim*), from the same root as the word for a womb — the ache a mother feels for the child she is carrying.

And that last sentence — "If I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved" — is שָׁכֹלְתִּי שָׁכָלְתִּי (*shacholti shachalti*), a construction that lets go. Long afterwards Esther says, "if I perish, I perish", and the tone of it is exactly the same.
Brothers and sisters, this is the greatest single turn Jacob makes in his entire life.
His name means grasp. He grasped at the birthright, he grasped at the blessing, he grasped at Laban's flocks, and he grasped that angel in the dark and would not let go. In this chapter, he lets go.
And notice the way he lets go. He prays and he prepares the gift at the same time; he entrusts the matter to God and he does the thing that has to be done, both at once.

Letting go is not letting things drop. Entrusting is not washing your hands. A person of faith still has to finish his homework — he simply knows that once it is finished, the outcome is not in his hands.

And this is what letting Jesus be King actually means: handing over the one person I cannot bear to lose. You and I each have a "Benjamin" inside us — the person or the thing you hold most tightly, the one you absolutely cannot afford to lose. Sometimes God is not asking to take him away. He is asking you to open your hand, so that he can get to work.
"If I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved" — is that despair, or is that faith?

In Hebrew it is a construction that lets go; long afterwards Esther says, "if I perish, I perish", and the tone is exactly the same. This is the greatest single turn Jacob makes in his whole life: his name means grasp — he grasped at the birthright, he grasped at the blessing, he grasped at Laban's flocks, he grasped that angel in the dark and would not let go — and in this chapter he opens his hand. And notice that before he lets go he calls on God Almighty, the name God used when he cut his covenant with Abraham in chapter 17 and when he spoke to Jacob at Bethel in chapter 35. So this is not resignation. It is giving the matter back to the God who had once spoken to him. Despair has nobody to address. Entrusting has somebody to address.
He prays and prepares a gift at the same time. Does that not show a shortage of trust?

Quite the opposite — this is exactly what maturity looks like. He takes the choice fruits of the land, he takes double money, he sends back the money that had been returned, and he even gives the other side a way out of the awkwardness: "Perhaps it was an oversight." Every one of those is a piece of thoroughly practical homework. And then he says, "May God Almighty give you mercy before the man." Letting go is not letting things drop; entrusting is not washing your hands. A person of faith still has to finish his homework — he simply knows that once it is finished, the outcome is not in his hands. That distinction is very useful in practice: to entrust and not act is laziness wearing spiritual clothes; to act and not entrust is propping the whole thing up by yourself until you collapse.
3. The Steward Says: Peace Be to You
They reach Egypt, and they are brought into Joseph's house. The text says, "The men were afraid."

Why would you be afraid of being invited to dine at a great man's house? Because there is something on your conscience. They say, "Because of the money that was returned in our sacks the first time, we're brought in; that he may seek occasion against us, attack us, and seize us as slaves, along with our donkeys."
"Seek occasion against us" is לְהִתְגֹּלֵל עָלֵינוּ (*lehitgolel aleinu*), literally "to roll himself down upon us" — the picture is of a great stone coming down on top of you.
They stop the steward at the door and explain themselves, sentence by careful sentence: the money has been brought back "in full weight", not a gram of it missing.
And then the steward says something extraordinarily beautiful:
"Peace be to you. Don't be afraid. Your God, and the God of your father, has given you treasure in your sacks. I received your money." (Genesis 43:23)
"Peace be to you" is שָׁלוֹם לָכֶם (*shalom lachem*) — peace be upon you. It is the first sentence the Lord Jesus spoke to his disciples after he rose from the dead.
"Don't be afraid" — אַל־תִּירָאוּ (*al-tira'u*) — is the most frequently repeated word of comfort in the whole Bible.
And "treasure" is מַטְמוֹן (*matmon*). That is not "here is your money back." That is buried treasure, riches hidden away for you.
And then the sentence that matters most of all: "I received your money."
Brothers and sisters, that one sentence is quite simply the gospel.

They are carrying an account they cannot balance, and they have brought double money in the hope of covering it. And the true master of the house says: that account — on my side, it has already been settled.

We do the same thing constantly. We carry a debt towards God inside us, and we set about covering it with more service, more giving, a better performance. But the one on the cross said, "It is finished!"
The account is settled. That bag of double money in your hand — you can put it down.

Then the steward brings Simeon out to them, and gives them water, and they wash their feet — that is the highest courtesy a household can offer a traveller from far away, exactly what Abraham did for his guests at Mamre. And seventeen hundred years later, at a last supper, there is another who takes water and washes his disciples' feet. Foot-washing has only ever run one way: the host does it for the guest, never the guest for the host.

There is one more detail worth noticing. When they stop the steward at the door to explain themselves, what they say is, "we indeed came down the first time to buy food" — and once again the Hebrew is the emphatic construction. They had rehearsed that speech the whole way down and packed double money to back it up, and in the end not one line of it was needed. When grace arrives, the reasons we have prepared usually turn out to be surplus to requirements.
Why were they afraid of being invited to dine at a great man's house?

Because there was something on their conscience. They said, "Because of the money that was returned in our sacks the first time, we're brought in; that he may seek occasion against us, attack us, and seize us as slaves." That phrase "seek occasion against us" is literally "to roll himself down upon us" — the picture of a great stone coming down on top of you. Here we see it once more: grace landing on a heart that owes something gets read as a trap. And the steward's answer is the most beautiful sentence in the chapter: "Peace be to you. Don't be afraid … I received your money." In Hebrew it opens with *shalom lachem*, peace be to you — the first words the Lord Jesus said to his disciples after he rose from the dead. The debt has already been paid by somebody else. That is the shape of the gospel.
4. Seated in the Order of Their Birth
Joseph comes home at noon. They present the gift, and "bowed themselves down to the earth before him" — twice over in this chapter they bow. The dream comes true once again.
Joseph's first question is this: "Is your father well, the old man of whom you spoke? Is he yet alive?"
"The old man" — he does not dare say "my father." Here is the prime minister of Egypt, standing in front of his own family, and he cannot say the words "my dad" without going the long way round.
Then he sees Benjamin. The text goes out of its way to add a footnote: "his mother's son" — of all Jacob's children, Rachel bore only the two of them.
And he says, "God be gracious to you, my son." In Hebrew that is אֱלֹהִים יָחְנְךָ (*Elohim yochnecha*), from the same root as the priestly blessing of Numbers 6.
"Joseph hurried, for his heart yearned over his brother; and he sought a place to weep. He entered into his room, and wept there." (Genesis 43:30)

"His heart yearned" is נִכְמְרוּ רַחֲמָיו (*nichmeru rachamav*), literally "his compassions were heated" — the inward parts churning, the heart burning like a fire. And that is the very same word, "mercy", that Jacob prayed for back in verse 14.
The father asked God Almighty to give them mercy. At this very moment that mercy is burning in the chest of the prime minister of Egypt.
"He sought a place to weep" — the second man in all Egypt has to go looking for somewhere to cry. This is the second time Joseph weeps.

And then: "He washed his face, and came out. He controlled himself, and said, 'Serve the meal.'" "He controlled himself" is וַיִּתְאַפַּק (*vayitapaq*), literally "he held himself in", the way hoops hold a barrel together.
Brothers and sisters, that is the actual daily life of a great many leaders: go inside and have your cry, wash your face, come back out and say, "Serve the meal."
And then comes the finest detail in the whole chapter:
"They sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his youth, and the men marveled with one another." (Genesis 43:33)
Eleven men to be arranged in order of birth — how many possible arrangements are there? Eleven factorial: getting on for forty million of them.
He got it right at the first attempt. No wonder "the men marveled with one another" — the Hebrew means they were struck dumb with astonishment.
You can be sure of what was going through their minds: how does this man know?

Brothers and sisters, this is the clue Joseph leaves them, and it is the comfort this chapter leaves us: there is One who knows everything about you. He knows where you come in the family. He knows the order of things in your house. He knows the details you have never told a living soul.
And the last verse says, "Benjamin's portion was five times as much as any of theirs. They drank, and were merry with him."

Twenty-two years ago, one coat of many colours was enough to make them plot murder. Today the youngest openly receives five times as much as anybody else, and they still eat together and are glad together.
This family is finally able to be glad together over one of its own. That is what Joseph was really watching for.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
There are several places in this chapter that need handling with care in the pulpit.

The first distortion is to preach Judah's standing surety as though a human being could atone for somebody else. Judah is a type, not the substitute himself; the one who truly bears the blame forever is the Lion who came out of his tribe. Blur the two and the congregation will walk away believing that one person can atone for another. The test is this: did they see a type, or did they see a substitute?

The second is to preach "letting go" as though it meant you need not care any more. After Jacob lets go he still prays, he still prepares the gift, he still sends the money back. Letting go is not letting things drop. Preach it the wrong way round and your congregation will mistake indifference for faith.

The third is to skate past the detail of the seating in order of birth. One chance in forty million — that is the clue Joseph deliberately drops. Leave it out and you have left out the enormous comfort inside it: there is One who knows everything about you.

The fourth is to preach Jacob's gift and his double money as a failure of faith. While he was preparing them, he was also saying, "May God Almighty give you mercy before the man." The two can stand together. Scold him for it and your congregation will conclude that making preparations is itself a form of unbelief.

The fifth is to preach Judah's change as though he had always been a good man underneath and had merely been muddled for a while. The text is honest about him: he proposed selling his own brother, and he committed a grave sin at the side of a road. His change began after the evidence was laid down in front of him and he owned that one sentence — "She is more righteous than I." Grace does not say he was good all along. Grace says he can be different.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: in a team, we are extremely good at not committing ourselves. Everyone sits in silence through the meeting, and then somebody says, "Look, let's do it this way — you go"; and when the thing falls apart, everybody says, "I said right at the start we shouldn't have done it like this." Service in the church, family business, a project at the company — it goes the same way every time. Brothers and sisters, whether a body of people has life in it can be measured by one thing: whether anybody is willing to say, "Put it on my account." This week, take responsibility for one thing on your own initiative instead of pushing it onto someone else. You do not have to carry all of it. You only have to be the first one to open his mouth.

The second question: we find it very hard to be genuinely glad about somebody else's good fortune. Especially our peers, our fellow workers, the children of relatives. On the surface we offer congratulations; inside we are taking measurements. In the last verse of this chapter, Benjamin's portion is five times as much as anybody else's, and the ten older brothers still eat together and are merry together. That is the real evidence that this family has been healed. Whether a family or a team can be built up does not depend on whether the gifting is there; it depends on whether we can be glad together over one person. This week, be genuinely glad once over somebody's good news — make one phone call and say the words, "I am so happy for you."
7. Living 321 Out — Put It on My Account
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. Judah said, "I'll be collateral for him … then let me bear the blame forever." And the Lion who came out of the tribe of Judah really did bear our blame forever: "He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree." This is my role model — he did not put up somebody else as security. He put up himself.

The Bible is my standard. The standard is not "protect yourself first." The standard is, "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ." Feelings say, "That is not my responsibility." The standard says that love "doesn't seek its own way."

The Holy Spirit is my guide. When to carry a thing and when to let it go — that takes guidance. If Jacob had gone on gripping Benjamin, the whole household would have starved; if he had let go carelessly, that would have been irresponsible. Rely on our intellect and lean on ourselves, and all you get is worry — you will be calculating the risk over and over. Rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit, and you get gladness — he will let you know that what had to be done is done, and the rest goes to him.

Let Jesus be King. "If I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved" — that is handing sovereignty back to God Almighty. Letting Jesus be King includes handing over the one person I cannot bear to give up. The person you are gripping so hard never actually belonged to you in the first place.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The steward says, "Your God, and the God of your father, has given you treasure in your sacks." It was Joseph who gave the order to put it there — and the steward hands the glory to God. When even the staff of a household have learned to give the credit to God, you may be quite sure that is how the man over them lives.

Establish God's system. The brothers are seated in the order of their birth, and not one of them envies the one who is given five times as much. Establishing God's system begins where we stop envying one another — because the enemy of the system has never been the difficulty outside. It is the comparing inside.
What is the "Benjamin" in each of our hearts?

It is the person or the thing you hold most tightly, the one you absolutely cannot afford to lose — a particular child, a particular relationship, a particular job, a particular position. The lesson of this chapter is not that God means to take him away; it is that he is asking you to open your hand, so that he can get to work. In practice there is a very simple test you can apply: if this one thing were gone, would my faith still be standing? If the answer is "that would be the end of me", then that one thing is already sitting on the throne. What letting Jesus be King actually means is handing over the one person I cannot bear to lose — not that I love him less, but that I stop treating him as my security.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Table
We come and sit down at that table carrying four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "Why on earth should I be the one to carry this?" Reuben's way was to put somebody else up as security; Jacob's way was to wait for other people to think of something. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights — wanting the deciding vote and not the responsibility. Humility is returning to our originally intended position as human beings and saying, "Put it on my account" — and in this family, nobody had said that sentence for twenty-two years.

The fearful heart says, "If I open my hand, he will be gone." Jacob was afraid for twenty-two years. But if he does not open his hand, the whole household starves. Fear does the arithmetic of loss; faith looks at God Almighty. And remember how it ends: after he lets go, not only does Benjamin come back — Joseph comes back too.

The ashamed heart says, "I was invited in to dinner, and all I could feel was fear." So did they. To a person carrying a debt inside, even grace looks like a trap. So listen to what that steward says: peace be to you, don't be afraid, I received your money. That account — somebody has already paid it for you.

The wounded heart says, "In this family I have never once been seen." And at that table sits a man who got the birth order of eleven brothers right at the first attempt. There is One who knows your place in the line, your position in the room, and the grievance you never said out loud. You thought nobody knew. In fact there is One who has known all along.
Four kinds of heart, one table. And the one who laid that table is the brother they sold.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, before God. Take the person you are gripping most tightly, name him out loud, and put him into the hands of God Almighty. When you pray, say the sentence out loud: "Lord, he is yours."
Second, before yourself. Go back over the last time you pushed something away — that "then you go", that "this isn't what I'm responsible for" — and say it over again in a different sentence.
Third, before other people. Take responsibility for one thing on your own initiative, instead of pushing it onto somebody else. Just one thing — and carry it all the way through.
Fourth, in your daily living. This week, be genuinely glad once over somebody else's good news. Ring them, send them a message, and say the words: "I am so happy for you."

Fifth, before your calling. Take one matter you intend to see through to the end and make God a concrete promise about it: what the thing is, how far you will take it, and when you will check up on yourself.

Sixth, tell one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a man in the Bible who sold his own younger brother when he was young. Second: twenty-odd years later he said to his father, "I'll be collateral for him … let me bear the blame forever." Third: a man changes like that because somewhere in between he admitted once that he was wrong — and that is the thing I have never been able to forget.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that when it comes round to me, I will say, "Put it on my account", and not, "Then you go."
I declare that I will open my hand and place the one I can least bear to lose into the hands of God Almighty.
I declare that my account has been settled; I will not go on using double money to cover a debt the Lord has already paid.
I declare that I will be genuinely glad over other people's good, and that envy will no longer make its home in me.
I am meant to say "Put it on my account" once this week, but I am afraid I will not be able to carry it. What should I do?

Define the scope first, so that taking responsibility does not turn into bravado. Three steps. First, take on only the part you can genuinely deliver, and write it down as one concrete sentence: "This particular piece of the job is mine, and if it goes wrong I will deal with it." Second, say out loud what your deadline is and on what terms you will ask for help — who you will go to when you cannot carry it. That is not retreating; that is being responsible. Third, having said it, do it: better to take on something smaller than to write a cheque that bounces. What Judah staked was something he could genuinely afford to pay, and in chapter 44 he really did stand up and pay it. The weight of what a person carries is not measured by how big the words were. It is measured by whether he delivered.
There are three sentences in this chapter worth remembering for the rest of your life.

One is Judah's: "I'll be collateral for him … then let me bear the blame forever." One is Jacob's: "If I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved." And one is the steward's: "Peace be to you … I received your money."
One is taking responsibility. One is letting go. One is grace.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on other people, not on my circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because the one who truly said "I'll be collateral for him" is the Lion of the tribe of Judah; the one who truly handed over his only Son is the Father; and the one who truly settled that account is the voice on the cross that said, "It is finished!"

May God bless every one of us to become the person who is willing to say, "Put it on my account"; may we open our gripping hands and place what we love most into the hands of God Almighty; and may we, seated at the same table, be genuinely glad for the one beside us who is given five times as much. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear and settled mindset.
1. ★★★ Reuben put up somebody else as security; Judah put up himself. What is the difference between "Put it on my account" and "Then you go"?
2. ★★ Between selling a brother and trading himself for a brother there lies one admission of being in the wrong. Why is owning it the starting line and not the finishing line?
3. ★ Letting go is not letting things drop, and entrusting is not washing your hands. Which of those two are you more likely to fall into?
4. ★★ "If I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved" — a man who grasped all his life opens his hand. What does that say to you?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (somebody else ought to be carrying this), fearful (I am afraid that if I take it on I will not be able to carry it), ashamed (I have failed to deliver before), wounded (I am always the one carrying it and nobody ever thanks me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "I'll be collateral for him. From my hand will you require him." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Who, or what, is the "Benjamin" in your heart? Where is the hardest part of opening your hand?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The thing I could least bear to lose is …"
9. ★★ This week, in which matter will you say, "Put it on my account"? State clearly how far your responsibility goes and by when.

Leader's reminder: the questions in this section will touch a deep dependence on a child, a spouse or a job. Do not say, "You care about it too much." If someone speaks about the fear of losing, stay with him first, and follow up privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, what is the one thing nobody has ever picked up and carried? Which part of it will you take on this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your service, which sentence of push-back gets used most often?
12. ★★★ The practice of opening the hand: this week, when you pray for your "Benjamin", add one sentence — "Lord, he is yours." Say when you are going to pray it.

13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him the thing you are taking responsibility for this week, and ask him to check at the end whether you delivered. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a man in the Bible who, when he was young, proposed selling his younger brother, and twenty-odd years later another younger brother was the one in trouble. Second: this time he said to his father, "I'll be collateral for him. From my hand will you require him" — and what he put up was himself. Third: so I believe that what shows whether a person has really changed is whether he is willing to say, "Put it on my account." Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the "Benjamin" in your heart, and the matter in which you will say "Put it on my account" this week. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to give us the faith to open our hands and the strength to carry what we have taken on.
